Delivery schedules are confirmed in your written quote, so ask for the current lead time before you plan around it.</p>[/vc_column_text][vc_column_text]<h2>What is the timeline from quote to finished building?</h2><p>The steps run in order, but several overlap. The manufacturing clock is only one of them.</p><ol class="bsb-steps"><li><strong>Quote and design.</strong> Confirm size, height, doors, and use.</li><li><strong>Engineered drawings.</strong> Drawings for your site’s snow, wind, and seismic loads.</li><li><strong>Permit.</strong> Submit to your county or city. Review time varies widely by jurisdiction.</li><li><strong>Order.</strong> The 8 to 10 week lead time starts here.</li><li><strong>Foundation.</strong> Poured and cured while your building is manufactured. This is the step most affected by frost.</li><li><strong>Delivery.</strong> Typically 8 to 10 weeks after order.</li><li><strong>Erection.</strong> Time depends on the size of the building and your crew.</li></ol>[/vc_column_text][vc_column_text]<h2>Why does frost and thaw timing matter in Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming?</h2><p>A foundation cannot be poured into frozen or saturated ground, and a building should not arrive before the slab or piers are ready. Valley sites often thaw earlier than mountain and high-plains sites. Work backward from your expected thaw date, then add the lead time.</p>[/vc_column_text][vc_column_text]<h2>Can you pour the foundation before the building arrives?</h2><p>Yes, and most buyers should. Anchor bolt layouts come from your engineered drawings, so complete those first.</p>[/vc_column_text][vc_column_text]<h2>What if you miss the spring window?</h2><p>You still have options.
